subsubtopic: PROTEST OF CANADIAN LEGION AGAINST CURTAILMENT OF HOLIDAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in answer I might say that last year it was enacted that Armistice day should be known as Remembrance day. It was hoped that (the public would fully obsei've the day, but some service was found to be necessary; this was only agreed to on the understanding that all returned soldiers, and others, would have opportunity given to attend services. In order adequately to meet the wishes of the public and those of the returned soldiers' organizations I have issued instructions to the effect that all postmasters are to be advised to restrict their services ito an absolute minimum. While postal employees are civil servants, and as such come under the Civil Service Act so far as the observance of holidays is concerned, yet the postal service is a public utility and, of neoessity, must operate in such a way as not to interfere unnecessarily with the carrying on of public business. A strict adherence to section 45 of the Civil Service Act would mean that no postal service whatever would be given on the days enumerated therein. I am given to understand that the legion representations would be met by instructions mentioned above, namely, that no delivery will be given unless absolutely essential and in that case restricted to the business section.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion now before the house, moved by the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) is for the purpose of endorsing the agreements which arose as a result of the deliberations of the gentlemen who took part in the Imperial economic conference in Ottawa last summer. The fact that the meeting at Ottawa was said to be an economic conference implies that it had for its purpose the solution of our economic ills. In examining the agreement now before us, therefore, we ask ourselves: To what extent, if any, does the agreement provide for the solution of our economic troubles? Do these agreements give any assurance to the Canadian workmen that in future they will be able to earn their bread by the sweat of their brow? The highest authority has decreed that in that manner man shall earn a livelihood. Only recently the heads of all churches denounced a system which has caused so much misery and distress to the human race. We must ask ourselves the question: Did the Imperial economic conference tackle these problems, or does the agreement now before us restore and expand the purchasing power of people within Canada and the empire? If not, then we must have with us unemployment and its attending miseries. Did the Imperial economic conference attempt to remove those conditions which are causing nations to strangle each other by tariffs, by quotas, by the juggling of exchange and in other restrictive ways? Surely we should ask ourselves whether or not these matters were considered because, on the one hand we see scientifically equipped factories capable of providing for every human being a much higher standard of living than obtains to-day. We see, further, that providence has provided us with natural resources in abundance. Those natural assets were provided not for the benefit of a few but for the good of the whole of mankind.
On the other hand despite the equipment in our factories we know that many are closed down, some working only 25 per cent or 50 per cent of their capacity. We see our fellow Canadian citizens out of work, in distress and misery. Many of them are at the point of desperation, knowing not from where their next meal may come. They are only a part of the millions throughout the world who find themselves in a similar plight. If the conference was not called to help those people, if it failed to remedy these injustices, I am afraid parliamentary language prohibits me expressing my opinion in connection therewith. If the conference did not tackle the problem I can say in parliamentary language that the conference was called under false pretences, that it was carried out with the intention of deceiving, and therefore it is not only a fraud and a failure but results in the disregard and betrayal of the rights of the masses of our people.
Having said that I purpose, in the few moments at my disposal, to examine the United Kingdom agreement and to see wherein the farmers and labouring men of Canada may secure any benefits, or in what manner they are protected. Members of the government have stated that as a result of the agreement trade now going to other parts of the world will be transferred to the empire. They state that as a result the British working men will secure more work. I am interested primarily in the Canadian working man, but my view is not so restricted that I cannot show interest in the problems of British labour. If the agreement is intended to give more work to the British working men why did not the Canadian government insist that the agreement should provide for 100 per cent British labour content? We give only 25 per cent Canadian content. Up to the present time we demand only 50 per cent British labour, content. We have heard the accusations to the effect that the British industrialist has his goods fabricated in cross-channel countries, brings them to Britain for finishing, and puts them on the Canadian and dominion markets as goods of British origin. At a time like this when we are making an agreement for five years surely we should protect the British workingmen at least to that extent. The very fact that this point has been omitted from the agreement leaves doubt in my mind as to whether or not British workingmen will receive any benefits.
Is it fair that the members of this house should be asked to vote on these agreements in toto first, and then afterwards, when we

What benefit is to be
derived from these agreements by our pulp and paper industries? This industry depends largely upon exports to the United States and it has found it impossible to prosper under Conservative policies. A comparison of Liberal and Conservative administrations shows that in 1923 there were 20,000,000

hundredweight of newsprint exported from this country; by 1930, still under Liberal administration, these exports rose to 44,000,000 hundredweight but by 1932, after two years of Conservative policies, these exports had dropped to 39,000,000 hundredweight. The wages of the men employed have been reduced and I say that the policies of the Conservative party have been harmful to this industry in my part of the country. As a member from northern Ontario I am asked to endorse these general agreements and then examine them afterwards.
What provision has been made in these agreements for a national fuel policy? The Prime Minister has stated that he would establish such a policy, but let us inquire how the mining industry of Nova Scotia has been getting along under the policies of this government. In round figures, in 1929, under a Liberal administration, 7,000,000 tons of coal were mined in Nova Scotia; in 1930, with a Conservative government in power for half the year, 6,000,000 were mined, and still under Conservative government, in 1931, which is the last figure I have, 4,000,000 tons were mined.
I have under my hand copy of a resolution sent to the Prime Minister from the miners of Nova Scotia, showing the distress and suffering that prevail in that locality. It goes on to show the number of women who are in a delicate state of health, undernourished, without sufficient clothing and requiring medical attention; the number of children who, under present conditions, are unable to attend school, and so forth. It is a heart-rending document to read. They finish up by saying that the miners of Nova Scotia are getting thirteen cents a head direct relief while it takes from forty-five to ninety cents per day to feed convicted thieves and murderers in this country. The document shows the situation among the miners of Nova Scotia. With the capacity that we have to produce by machinery in ever-greater abundance, I ask:	Was any effort made at
the imperial conference, because I refuse to call it an economic conference any more, to ensure a shorter working day in Canada or within the empire? Was any provision made for the more equitable distribution of the wealth of Canada or of the empire especially in relation to those matters pertaining to the maintenance of health, comfort and happiness? These machines which are now taking the place of working men, were purchased out of the profits made by good, loyal, efficient workmen in Canada and within the British Empire. Consideration therefore has been given only to the question of profits

and dividends, and no consideration has been given to the men who produce. X am not surprised at this, because, so far as Canada is concerned, this government refused to tolerate any labour advice in connection with the conference. Was the question of unemployment or how we were to take care of the unemployed men and women throughout Canada discussed at the conference? If it was not, why not? The attitude of the Prime Minister this afternoon in his reply to a question raised by the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) would indicate that it is one of the last things he would discuss in the House of Commons, let alone a conference. So, having these thoughts in mind and having these documents before me for ratification, after giving the matter consideration, and having an interest in and representing the workers and farmers in my constituency, I could not possibly assent to or support the principles upon which these agreements are based.
The Prime Minister, in concluding his remarks the other day, resorted to poetry. We can all recall it. I am not a poet, but I think what he ought to have had in mind and what would be more appropriate to the occasion would be along these lines: In 1930 the Tory party was made mighty by deceiving the Canadian electors, and now hope by bluff, bluster, ballyhoo and buncombe to become even mightier yet.
Mr. IV. T. LUCAS (Camrose):	Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention at this time to discuss at any great length the agreement now before the house. I believe it has already been carefully analysed by both sides, and therefore no particular advantage will be gained by reiterating what has previously been said, thus prolonging the debate. Having listened to the arguments pro and con and having carefully studied the agreement,
I have come to a definite decision as to how I shall vote on this question, and I therefore feel it is only fair to the house that I should indicate my reasons for so doing.
May I first, however, be permitted to say that with the arguments of those who advocate greater freedom of world trade, I heartily agree, but here again one has to deal with facts rather than with a theory. It cannot be said that the present high tariffs of the world were put up in retaliation for the action of Canada or of Great Britain. In fact we find that those barriers were put up and the doors almost closed to our trade when a Liberal government was in office in Canada and while Great Britain was yet a free trade country. I think hon. members will agree with me that conditions must
have been very serious in Great Britain when that country decided to abandon its free trade policy which had been in existence for almost a century. In my opinion they had no choice in the matter but were simply forced by a set of new conditions to make the change. May I ask hon. members, knowing conditions as they exist to-day, with the industrial development which has taken place in every country in the world and with the piled up surplus goods which are looking for an outlet at distress prices: in all sincerity could Canada tear down her tariff barriers and become the dumping ground of the world while those other markets remained barred to us? These are cold, hard facts which have to be faced whether we like them or not. It was because of such conditions that the empire countries, finding themselves barred from those world markets, met in Ottawa in July last in an attempt to bring about better trade relations among themselves. It is my belief that the action of Great Britain in adopting a tariff policy will hasten the day when we may look for a lowering of tariff barriers all around.
Science and invention are bringing the world closer and closer together and while our ultimate goal is a world confederation, the day for that has not yet arrived. In my opinion the development towards that goal is from the small to the ever larger, growing unit. Within the last fifty years we have seen that development clear and distinct. First we had the small village unit, almost self-contained, with the different craftsmen plying their various trades and supplying the needs of the community. Second, we had the small town factory, and the village craftsman disappeared. Third, we had the age of the combine and merger when the small factory was swallowed up and our great industries located in our larger cities. At present we are organized as national units. This is what has happened. Following along the same line, the next logical step to form again a larger unit is a combination of nations such as the British commonwealth of nations which was furthered and strengthened by such a gathering as we had in Ottawa last summer. The United States is large enough to form such a unit; in fact, it is an empire within itself and I am of opinion that we shall next see a confederation of the states of Europe-and after this has run its course, finally a world confederation. The condition which Tennyson so beautifully pictured in that prophetic poem Locksley Hall:
Not in vain the distance beacons. Forward, forward let us range,
Let the great world spin forever down the ringing grooves of change.

Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements_
And again:
Till the war-drum tlirobb'd no longer and the battle-flags are furl'd
In the parliament of man, the federation ol the world.
The hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), very fair and moderate as usual, in his speech in this debate pictured a development somewhat similar to the one I have endeavoured to portray; but he viewed such a development with fear, fear of the results. But I have no fears, Mr. Speaker. In fact, I look to this very form of development to hasten the day we all desire to see. Just as it would have been impossible to have jumped all at once from the small village unit to the national unit we have today, so it would be impossible for the many national units throughout the whole world to form at once one harmonious whole. Before that can be accomplished we shall have to develop more of the spirit of brotherhood and cooperation, and I believe that this can best be achieved by a grouping together of those peoples more or less similar in character, and then when they have learned to cooperate within their own sphere there will be greater hope of the larger world groups getting together to form a world confederation.
No one will deny that the British Empire has been a very potent factor down through the ages in the development of our world civilization. It has stood as an example of liberty and justice, and anything that will tend to strengthen the empire so that it may continue in these days of stress and tribulation to point the way to peace and a better understanding amongst the peoples of the world will have my support. I am sure that no one who listened to that very earnest address delivered a few days ago by Earl Reading could help but feel that with such men to guide and direct the empire there was at least some reason for hope, and that the influence of such an empire upon the world at large could have only beneficial results.
I have also a profound admiration for that great statesman who headed the British delegation to the recent Ottawa conference, the Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin. Not the polished type of .orator, but the earnest, capable thinker, who in beautiful and simple language impresses everyone with his great sincerity of purpose. Those who heard him speaking at the Canadian Club during the conference will remember that he said: We are building for eternity and the ultimate goal of man is the kingdom of heaven here upon earth. I have

always been impressed by the statement that he made at the Imperial conference in 1926:
We had been taunted in the past with being an aggressive race. If ever the lust for dominion possessed us, that phase has passed. We are a league of nations within ourselves, devoted to the cause of peace.
We seek to improve the methods of peaceful intercourse with foreign nations, holding ourselves together one-quarter of the human race. If we can make the bounds of freedom in the world yet wider, if we can faithfully discharge our responsibilities to civilization-to civilizations other than our own, which exist in Asia, in Africa, and in the islands of the seas-then, indeed, our empire can be justified to the world today and justified to posterity. On those foundations and on those foundations alone it will endure.
Then he quoted that age-old motto:
In essentials unity; in non-essentials, liberty; in all things, charity.
It was the practising of such a motto, Mr. Speaker, that enabled the British people in days gone by successfully to colonize and develop her dominions, and anything that can be done to further those ends by knitting closer the bonds of empire, thus developing and strengthening the spirit on which it wras founded, should have our support.
In furtherance of this unit development, Mr. Speaker, the empire countries came together in July last. The delegates were all chosen in our best known democratic manner, and may I pause here to say that I believe they were as sincere a body of men as could be found anywhere, and that they did not come to Ottawa with any ulterior purpose, but with the best interests of the empire at heart. But as these delegates were all human beings it was only natural that each group should want to make as good a bargain as possible for its own unit, and as no one could have everything and give nothing, it meant that there had to be compromise; and so if there are some things in the agreement which we do not like we may look upon them as the price we had to pay for the things we received.
I believe I am safe in saying that the greatest disappointment to the people cf Canada was the fact that the conference did nothing to stabilize exchange or to give any lead in regard to monetary reform. I heard many discussions before and during the sitting of the conference, and the consensus of opinion that I found was that while some advantages might be obtained in so far as trade was concerned, if only the exchange question was settled, and at least some lead given on the question of monetary reform, the conference would then have been well worth while, and

United Kingdom
there was certainly a very strong feeling of disappointment when the monetary committee of the conference made its report, and it was found that nothing of importance had been accomplished in these vital matters.
If we have found it necessary because of trade barriers placed against us by other countries to divert more of our trade to the United Kingdom then I think it is also necessary and very important that the payment for those goods exported should come direct through Canadian channels, instead of through New York, as it does at the present time. I believe that the time has come for Canada to establish some form of central bank, one of whose powers it would be to handle our exchange direct through Canadian channels, and I hope that the government will give due consideration to this suggestion.
While I am disappointed. Mr. Speaker, that no action was taken by the monetary committee of the conference, I realize the fact that to reject this treaty would have no effect on the exchange question, but would leave it just where it is at present. In fact, I believe that a solution of the exchange question will be found sooner by accepting this treaty, and for this reason: The government has staked its political future on these agreements. Now it is my opinion that the preferences which we are being granted in the British market will be almost if not completely nullified by the depreciated currency of other exporting countries, and so if Canada is to receive any actual benefit from these agreements the government will simply be forced to deal with the exchange question.
I understand that the Prime Minister took the ground that Russian dumping would nullify our proposed preferences in the British market. With this I heartily agree, and we are told that this dumping is to be stopped. But, Mr. Speaker, what difference does it make to a farmer or a lumber merchant in Canada if the preference is wiped out by Russian dumping or by ithe depreciated currency of some other country? The effect is just the same in either case, and therefore I feel certain that before Canada will receive any substantial benefit from the preferences which we are to obtain in the British market under this agreement the government will be forced to deal with the exchange question.
It is my opinion that Canadian agriculture should receive some benefits from these agreements and under the conditions with which we are confronted today, conditions which I shall not attempt to describe because they have been ably depicted by many former speakers, agriculture will certainly need some stimulus. I
doubt very much if the six cents per bushel will appreciably raise the price of wheat, but I wonder in what position we would be if that six cents were against us. I must say I have been very much amused by some of the arguments of hon. members to my right who have stated definitely that the six cent preference will be of no benefit. Then, almost in the same breath they have shown great concern about the grain to be shipped through the United States, for fear it may not come under the agreement and thereby receive the benefit of it. If they are sincere in their argument that the six cent preference is of no use, why worry about the manner in which grain is to be shipped?
I believe Canadian farmers will receive a distinct advantage in so far as removal of restrictions on cattle are concerned, and also to the pig, poultry and dairy industries. Canada will be afforded an opportunity to develop trade in these commodities. Whether or not we accept the opportunity now afforded us remains entirely with ourselves. If full advantage is to be derived I believe that the government will have to create at once an export marketing board with very wide powers, one with power to control the full shipping space for cattle so that no middle man may step in and reap a toll on every head of cattle shipped. Cooperative agencies should be formed as collection and shipping agents so as to give competition to our private packing companies in order that they may not reap the full benefits at the expense of the farmer. Further, such a board should encourage the development of trade iu order that a continuity of supply may be assured the British market.
After giving careful consideration to the agreement now before us it is my belief that if the measure is carried advantage will accrue to Canadian agriculture, to the lumber and mining industries. If rejected, however, what is the alternative? Last year Great Britain changed her whole fiscal policy when she passed what is known as the Import Duties Act. Under this act a ten per cent duty was levied on all imports from foreign countries, with the exception of a limited free list. Empire products were exempted until November 15 of this year so that the dominions could have time to negotiate preferential treaties with the United Kingdom. The goods of any dominion not reaching an agreement by that date will be treated as coming from a foreign country and will be subject to the Import Duties Act. So that there may be no mistake as to the position taken by
702	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
British statesmen, and in answer to hon. members who argue otherwise, I should like to quote a statement made by Hon. J. H. Thomas in the British House of Commons on October 26, 1932. A Canadian Press despatch of that date states as follows:
The Irish Free State will lose the advantage of impex-ial tariff preferences in the United Kingdom on November 15. J. H. Thomas, Dominions Secretary, told the House of Commons today. On that date, he explained, preferences granted goods from the dominions under last year's tariff act will expire, and as the Free State failed to conclude any trade agreement with the United Kingdom at the Ottawa economic conference, its exports to Great Britain will be accorded tariff treatment similar to that affecting goods from foreign countries.
Then the correspondent goes on to explain:
Under the Tariff Act a general 10 per cent duty was levied on all imports from foreign countries with the exception of a limited free list. Empire products, including those of the Free State, were exempted until November 15 of this year. Meanwhile difficulties arose between the United Kingdom and the Free State over the land annuities question, and the United Kingdom imposed a special 20 per cent duty on imports of Free State goods such as live animals for food, butter, eggs, cream, bacon, pork, poultry, game and meats. At that time, however, the general 10 per cent preference was continued.
The article continues:
Mr. Thomas made his announcement as he moved second reading of the Ottawa agreements bill which will give effect to trade pacts concluded between the United Kingdom and the dominions. The bill when passed will continue preferences on goods from empire countries, except those from the Free State.
The net result will be that all goods imported to the United Kingdom from the Free State except those on the free list of the Tariff Act, will be charged the regular duty of 10 per cent, while those already assessed 20 per cent under the special duties will be charged an additional 10 per cent.
In making the announcement Mr. Thomas said, "AAre deplore that there is one dominion which by her own actions has deprived herself of the Ottawa agreements, but I wish to say on behalf of the government we hope it is only temporary."
The hon. member for North AA7aterloo (Mr. Euler) admitted that while the conditions described in this newspaper article may be true, Canada held an effective weapon by which, in the event of her goods being denied entry to the British market, she could remove the British preferential rate on British goods entering Canada. While that may be true, it is that very action we do not wish to take, and I wager the hon. member would rather support the treaty, even if it were less favourable to Canada, than to have such a condition brought about.

I fully appreciate the fact that the passing of the Canada-United Kingdom agreement will not afford a panacea for all our ills, but at least it may lay a foundation upon which we may build for the future. While this agreement may not be all we should like it to be, and as only time can fully demonstrate its value I think it should be given a fair trial. As a farmer representative with full knowledge of how other world markets are barred against us, I could not conscientiously vote to place restrictions upon the one great free market now open to our products. Therefore I shall vote for the agreement.
Mr. CAMERON R. McINTOSH (North Battleford):	Mr. Speaker, I listened carefully to the remarks of the last speaker, the hon. member for Camrose (Mr. Lucas), and if I did not miss the point he was trying to drive home I gathered that he stood for still higher tariffs for western Canada. AA7ell. Mr. Speaker, I do not; I never did, and I do not intend to thus betray my constituents in the future. I shall oppose this trade agreement, and that is one reason for my opposition, and one reason why I intend to vote against it.
Then I noticed the hon. member depicted in rather splendid phraseology the coming federation of the world under a Tory policy and Tory principles. I do not believe there is the faintest possibility of achieving that end. I do not think there is a chance for the nations of the world to be harmoniously drawn together under a policy such as that outlined in this trade agreement. I believe nations will be torn asunder by it if we are not vigilant, and instead of unification and harmony there will be recrimination, disharmony and discontent.
AVith these few remarks I should like to pass on to the matter of the motion for the ratification of the treaty. I believe I have already in this question defined my attitude. I can see nothing of any account in the treaty which merits my support. In fact, when I balance the good with the bad appearing in it my immediate conclusion is that I must oppose it. I oppose it not only on behalf of my constituency, but also on behalf of that section of Canada I represent, namely, western Canada. No matter what riding I represented in this house I could not do other than oppose the treaty now before us. I dhall later give some of the reasons for the position which, as a responsible member of this chamber I must take in this matter.
Up to the present time there has been a splendid debate and, Mr. Speaker, I must

United Kingdom
say it reminds me very much of a baseball match. The Prime Minister went to bat first and, with full knowledge of the trade agreement, being in intimate touch with it from its inception until the time the signatures were attached, and having nursed it from one week to another, he came to the house and made a very commendable presentation. I should say he made a home run-scrambled across the home plate. But although the Prime Minister said he was embarking on a new empire policy-and I think he is, and a dangerous one for Canada too-and although he said "we have done well," I cannot see any remarkable enthusiasm on the part of his followers since the first day the treaty was introduced into the house. We have only had what you might call a straggling debate; we have not had as far as government supporters are concerned a debate on the merits of the matter at all. This is a momentous question; in many respects we are at the crossroads in the history of the empire. A few timid debaters on the other side of the house have risen to support the Prime Minister, who did make a home run, and who had every opportunity to do so. Personally I should like to have seen more hon. members who sit behind the Prime Minister, especially those from western Canada, get up and tell their ridings why they are supporting this agreement. Let them, as we are endeavouring to do, inform their electors on that question, and we will see what will happen to those hon. gentlemen later when the election rolls around.

speechtext:
Does my hon. friend say we shall never hear of him after another election? If so, I think he is about telling the truth. My belief is that within another decade there will not be a high tariff government left in the world. I believe the great fight going on now across the international boundary means only one thing; it means the defeat of a party that for years has stood for out and out high protection, and although the party opposing them has not definitely stated that it will lower tariffs,-they know that would be politically dangerous at present,- when it is returned to power there will be a definite move in that direction, there is no doubt of that. And so it will be all over the world. The present government in Great Britain stands for higher tariffs on raw materials and food stuffs, but it will never see daylight in the next election. Those two great nations with additions will make a girdle around the world as far as freer trade is concerned. Then we shall have an opportunity to do something for the common people by bringing down measures looking not only toward freer trade, but also toward vital reforms in other directions.
After the Prime Minister had his say in the debate, the official opposition in the house continued the discussion, and the right hon. leader of the Liberal opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), may be said to have made a home run as did the Prime Minister. The right hon. leader of the opposition simply took the arguments presented by the head of the government and demolished them. From then on the debate on this side of the house, including the southeast corner, has been, I would say, extremely useful. Our endeavour has been to bring out the principles involved in this treaty, and also to get before the country all the information possible with regard to it in order that the people may be armed with facts so that when the next appeal to them takes place we can have a definite decision one way or another in regard to spurious ultra-imperialistic ill-conceived treaties of this kind.
.Now, Mr. Speaker, may I say that in considering this pact we as a party stand for more and freer trade with the empire and the world. That, this treaty does not give, therefore we are not going to vote for it. We stand, I say, for freer trade with the empire and the world, not on narrow lines of exclusive nationalism and ultra-imperialism, but on the broad basis of a recognition of the world as the ultimate economic unit. That is our policy, and any treaty in opposition to such a policy we as a party will oppose and do our best to defeat. The ramifications of it may be as beautiful as the Prime Minister indicated, but the ramifications of a self-sufficient empire mean no more to me than the ramifications of a self-sufficient ultra-economic nationalism. Ultra-imperialism is just as dangerous and ugly as ultra-nationalism. The dominion and British parliaments it is conclusively shown in these treaties, dictate to the colonial empire what taxes they shall have to levy on their people, and the conditions on which they shall trade with the worid. That is not the way to build up an empire, because dictation by one part of the commonwealth of the fiscal policies of another simply means retrogression and resentment, not advancement or prosperity.
Let me read what the Manchester Guardian says about this empty treaty to which the government are pinning their faith as a fettering instrument of empire and nationhood.
704	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
The Manchester Guardian says that an "imperial partisan policy" has been forced on the country. That is a nice thing to have said across the north Atlantic. It also says that this treaty is "the culmination of extreme protectionist policy." Yet we have hon. members from western Canada defending a treaty of this kind which stands for extreme protectionism, as though we had not had enough of it. Then it goes on to say:
Every day that passes brings forth fresh evidence of the dangerous character of the Ottawa agreements, whether they are looked on narrowly as they affect British trade or more particularly as they affect the prospects of the revival of world trade.
Looked at from any angle you like, from the standpoint of nationalism, from the standpoint of Canada, from the standpoint of the empire, from the international standpoint, these treaties are not worth supporting. Then again the same paper says:
Ottawa has become a matter of derision rather than of serious argument outside any assembly but a public meeting of Tory politicians.
The Manchester Guardian says further that the treaty is the product of a conflict between the British government and the Canadian government and between British industries and Canadian industries. That is, it is a result of a conflict between the British government and the industries supporting that government in the old land, and the Canadian government backed by the invisible industrial government of this country that wants a higher tariff.
In the motion for ratification the Prime Minister asks us to ratify this treaty, subject of course to the fiscal changes consequent thereupon. In the amendment put forward by the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston) four or five main points are emphasized; first, that we would welcome any condition in the treaty that would tend to lower tariffs and help market the products of Canada in an international way; second, that we condemn any agreement which would increase an already unreasonably high tariff; third, that we disapprove of any treaty that would prevent us from exercising our rights to negotiate with other countries in a commercial way in order to secure favourable commercial treaties for the marketing of our goods beyond the seas; fourth, that we regret that there is nothing in the treaty to show that the government is doing away with order in council action restricting imports into Canada. And lastly, as of course any one would expect, the Liberal party reaffirms its stand on the

British preference, the foundation of all preferences in 1897 under our great leader, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, whose memory we shall ever revere. We know he laid the foundation of preferential imperialism, and we know that foundation was sound. It was voluntary, not involuntary; it was a preference secured not by haggling pressure or hard bargaining, but by good-will and mutual friendship. On that foundation we stand at the present time. I oppose the treaty, sir, for every one of the reasons mentioned in that amendment, which is in reality before the house.
May I go back for a moment to the pledges made by this party in the election of 1930? What did they say? They said they would foster and develop agriculture and the live stock and dairying industry. Have they fostered and developed these industries ? I would say they have fossilized and destroyed them. Agriculture to-day is the pity, not the admiration of the people of Canada, because thej1' know it is in a mess; and this is largely due to the fact that the party opposite has put it on the rocks in the last two years. Again, hon. gentlemen opposite pledged themselves to the stabilization of economic conditions and a continuity of opportunity and freedom from manipulation of tariffs at home and abroad. Well, we have never had such manipulation of tariffs in this country. We are not free from tariff manipulation, for we have had, in the last two years, more tariff manipulation than we have ever had in the history of Canada. Nor has there been any economic stabilization; on the contrary, the whole financial structure of the country is in danger today, because the party opposite two years ago gave the people a number of pledges not one of which they have attempted to fulfil. Further, they declared that they would develop interprovincial trade and secure foreign markets. Where are the foreign markets today, pray? We have not a paying foreign market today for our produce, not one. And where is the increased trade as between one province and another? Why, sir, our trade is almost down to the vanishing point. Hon. gentlemen opposite pledged themselves to foster, support and promote greater non-voluntary empire trade on the basis of haggling, or, as they say, mutual advantage. Their policy in this regard is found, of course, in this treaty; they think they will build up the largest possible volume of empire trade by this means, but I do not believe they will. Lastly, they said they would introduce compensating adjustments in the different provinces to make up for the high tariffs given to the industrialists. We know what they have done in that direction. For

United Kingdom
instance, the wheat problem, which I shall discuss presently, will show you just what compensating advantages the wheat growers of western Canada have received by reason of the extension of these tariffs to the industrialists. The fact is, they have received none.
Before this treaty was brought down in the house I was in some doubt about what its contents would be, and I had misgivings for the following reasons. In the first place, I was not unmindful of the pledges of hon. gentlemen opposite, which I have quoted to this house and not one of which has been redeemed. Again, I recalled that at the special session of 1930 this same Canada first tariff policy was put into operation and the government jerked up the tariff on about 170 items. That, of course, made me suspicious. Then in 1930 our Prime Minister went to London and, for the first time, turned the imperial conference into a " humbug " conference, so that no advancement was made at that conference in the direction of increased trade or lower empire tariffs. The only thing he did was to inculcate, or to try to inculcate in the minds of the British electorate a desire to adopt a protective tariff. We know Britishers have adopted it and now we are at the mercy of that tariff. Following this in the regular session of parliament in 1931 this high tariff policy was persisted in, with the result that the tariff was increased on over two hundred articles. That intensified my suspicions. So that, combining the special session of 1930 with the humbug conference and the session of 1931, I had every reason to be sceptical of the contents of this treaty which is now before us. But, more than that, there was the fact that no information was given to this house before the close of last session. We were asking for information every day with respect to the agenda of the conference, but no information was given us, with the result that we went home absolutely in the dark, knowing nothing whatever as to what was going to take place. The only information we could gather as to what was taking place in Ottawa in connection with the conference was such information as was given us through the medium of the press. Moreover, the iron and steel men got together and industrially carved up Canada, and other interests tried to do the same thing, but failed to agree. It turned out later on that the conference simply developed into a hive of factious and commercial rivalry. The industrial' interests of Canada were opposing the industrial interests of Great Britain; the government of Canada and the government of Great Britain were in fighting opposition, and in consequence we have this 53719-45
practically useless agreement which is now before us for consideration. We are told that
this treaty is a step in the direction of new and sound empire development, but I, for one, do not think it is.
May I point out that these treaties were signed by the government of Canada without the consent of the Canadian people or of parliament, and the only intimation we had as to what they contained was that in notice after notice that came from the daily and weekly press in connection with the conference-certain statements were vouchsafed to the public of Canada by the Minister of Railways. Well, we know what that information amounted to. It was really not solid information at all, it was largely worthless; and although a good many of these news items were disseminated throughout Canada, and editorial comment was based upon them, the people of Canada will now realize that much of that news and much of the editorial comment thereon was unsound. The result is that the people will have to do their thinking on these treaties all over again-a sad condition of affaire.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that this is very commendable; this is not the way to build up a strong and well-informed Canadian nationality. I do not believe it is the way to found a greater Canada, because it cannot be done. Subsequently the government went into the constituency of South Huron and fought a by-election. The contents of the treaty were then unknown and they tried to win a snap verdict there on it. With what result? They were beaten by a plurality of approximately 2,000. And that is as it should be. I believe that if the treaties had been presented to the electorate during that by-election the majority against the government would have been, not 2,000 but more like 4,000. Not only that, but one very great drawback to the conference, as I see it, is the fact that at that conference there was no direct representation for agriculture; neither the farming nor the labouring classes were represented. That ought not to be so. I believe that when we hold an empire conference, especially in Canada, we ought to hold a four-square conference, and our endeavour should be to prove to the people that we want to do business in the right way and that we are going to act squarely and in good faith toward all sections and industries of Canada, The government leaders were not actuated by these sentiments at the conference of last July and

706	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
August, nor are they embodied in the treaty now before the house.
But notwithstanding these doubts and suspicions, I did think that the Prime Minister and his government would at least rise to the occasion and endeavour to do something that would be of benefit to Canada as a whole. Why, Mr. Speaker, the price levels in Canada, in agriculture and in every other industry, constituted a challenge to any man who called himself a statesman; they were a challenge to any cabinet to take action and do something practical. Did this government do anything of a practical character? Not at all. The fact is, Mr. Speaker, that the trade of this country has dwindled to about one billion dollars, so that we are back where we were in 1911. At that time our trade amounted to about eight hundred million dollars, and now, as I say, it is about one billion. But that is not all; our trade is dwindling steadily, it is going down and down, and if this trend continues we shall find in a few years that we have no more trade-no more business. Moreover, the gap that exists today, just as it existed last July and August, between the prices which the farmers receive for their products and those which the industrialists get for theirs, should have been closed. The conference, however, did not make any move at all, either in a commercial or in a monetary way, to close that gap, with the result that the situation is becoming alarmingly worse. And what about the debt situation? The debt of this country is stupendous, while the prices of primary products have suffered enormously. How shall we ever obtain money with which to pay our debts in this dominion-our national debt, our provincial debts and our municipal debts? It cannot be done if we go on as we are; yet no move was made at the Imperial conference, that great gathering of empire statesmen, to effect a solution of this pressing problem. Nothing was done by the conference to meet this problem-absolutely nothing. As I say, I had my doubts, but I reserved judgment until I should find out what had been actually done to mitigate our debt burdens, but when the truth became known I found that no move had been made at all to meet the problem. Again, Mr. Speaker, the unemployment situation is one that would challenge any government; but no move was made either directly or indirectly to solve this problem. Unemployment is becoming worse; we have over 700,000 unemployed in the country; yet a conference like this is held and nothing is done to solve

a problem of such a serious character. Inasmuch as the conference was interpreted as a turning point in the history of Canada, as of the empire at large, one would fancy that the cabinet ministers, led by the Prime Minister, would at least have made some effort to live up to the high ideals of the Canadian people. But they did nothing of the kind. The Prime Minister and his associates refused to stand for lower tariffs, for a true reconstruction policy, and for principles that would make for a better and more prosperous Canada in the present day as well as for the future. On the whole, then, nothing was done and we are in the same dire position today as we were before we entered the conference.
These serious conditions were not faced and because of this the message to parliament of the Prime Minister did not contain much to instil confidence in the people of Canada. So in order to put the facts of this treaty before parliament, in order to have every aspect of the agreement presented to the electorate, in order to show why we are opposing this treaty on national and empire grounds, as the Liberal party of Canada we are carrying on this debate. We believe that when the particulars of this debate reach the average home in Canada, the conclusion of the average elector will be that this government has made one of the most critical blunders in its history.
Every Tory government has always been a high tariff government and when we look back to the days before and after confederation we realize the truth of this statement. Before confederation our average tariff was from 10 to 12 per cent; the Conservatives came into power and the tariff went up to 15 per cent-they said it was going to increase business-then between 1873 and 1878 there was another jump to 17^ per cent; then from 1878 to 1896, under Macdonald, it jumped from 20 to 30 per cent. The Conservative governments have always been trying to build up business with high tariffs, but let us consider the trade figures for these periods. It will be found that the total trade kept going down and down, just as it is doing today. When protection is raised beyond certain limits trade is discouraged and the whole burden is placed upon the primary producers. Buying power is cut to pieces and we are put on our backs financially and commercially-where we are at present.
The Liberals were in power from 1896 to 1911 and during that period they reduced tariffs by easily 5 per cent and adopted the voluntary preference idea. Leaving out the war, the next period was from 1921 to 1930, during which the tariffs remained about the

same, but from 1930 to 1932, under another Conservative government, the tariff has gone up in spots to 60 and 80 per cent to over 35 per cent on the average. Under Conservative governments 'the tariff is going up all the time-continuously.
The trade figures show that high tariffs do not develop trade. From 1868 to 1873 the increase in	trade	amounted to about
$91,000,000. From 1874 to 1878 there was a drop of $41,000,000, and from 1879 to 1896 there was an increase of $72,000,000. During the next fifteen years, under a Liberal regime with moderate tariffs and the British preference the trade increased by over $500,000,000, or within a few millions of our present trade. From 1923 to 1930 Canada had the highest per capita trade in her history. In 1929 the total was $2,654,000,000, it then dropped in 1931 to $1,700,000,000 and again in 1932 to $1,100,000,000. These figures demonstrate the destructive influence of high tariffs and yet this government continues with its policy which will surely put in danger the economic and commercial fabric of this country.
Let us consider wheat as a potential trading product for a few moments. Economically the business structure of western Canada is based on wheat. We grow other products, but wheat is the most important. Any move internationally which will cut down our wheat production rather than obtain a fair price for the producer is a move in the wrong direction. We should be enabled to exchange our goods for the goods of other countries; if tariffs were lowered and production costs decreased, then we could trade our wheat- economically produced-for the cheaply fabricated products of other than wheat producing countries. Any treaty which does not remedy present trading defects as explained will in time so undermine agriculture that prices will be forced still lower. How can farmers live on these prices? The cost of taking a bushel of wheat from North Battleford to the head of the lakes is 23 cents per hundredweight or 16.8 cents per bushel. The commission and elevator charges take up another five cents per bushel, which leaves the farmer about 24 or 25 cents per bushel for number one northern. How can any farmer buy the products of the factories of eastern Canada when wheat brings a price like this? Wheat cannot be produced for anything less than 55 cents to 87 cents a bushel.
According to this agreement we are to get a preferential protection of five or six cents a bushel on wheat entering the United Kingdom. However, article 4 reads as follows:
It is agreed that the duty on either wheat in grain, copper, zinc or lead as provided in this agreement may be removed if at any time empire producers of wheat in grain, copper, zinc and lead respectively are unable or unwilling to offer these commodities on first sale in the United Kingdom at prices not exceeding the world prices and in quantities sufficient to supply the requirements of the United Kingdom consumers.
We obtain this preference only so long as we are willing to supply the British Empire with all the wheat she wants. We have been told that the British market is a sheltered market, therefore it cannot be considered as a world market. Wheat will be sold on another world market and the price obtained there will be the price we will be paid for our wheat. I cannot see any benefit in the preference we are given because after all is said and done we must accept the world price as previously.

The next is from Mr. Schlieman, the reeve of the municipality of Round Hill, and reads:

These men have lost confidence in this treaty already if they ever had any. The next is from near Shellbrook, near Prince Albert, and reads:

The resolution passed by the council reads as follows:
Resolved that this council petition Dominion government, in view of dire stress of farmers and to extreme low price of grain, that government take immediate steps for granting of bonus to farmers of western Canada on 1932 wheat. It is our opinion that this step would create confidence of far-reaching nature and would result in payment of taxes local and government, and would place municipality in strong financial position and enable it to liquidate financial obligations and aid over-coming relief problem. In addition we are of opinion granting bonus provide immediate circulation money which would benefit many branches of industry and government.

Then I have another telegram from the North Battleford Board of Trade, and this is what the members of this august body have to say about the situation now:
Have wired the Right Hon. R. B. Bennett as follows at a meeting of the North Battleford Board of Trade Council held this evening. It was resolved that in view of the plight of grain growers

Note the word "plight."

in the western provinces that the federal government be urged to take into earnest consideration the question of granting a bonus to the said growers.
Shades of 1930! So I might go on. The farmers of the west are advocating a bonus. If they cannot get a bushel bonus, they want a certain value per acre for every acre sowed. They want a bonus or something of that nature because they realize that this treaty, when it goes into effect, is nullified because of the high protection principle under which the agreement operates and that so far as the preference in the British market is concerned, it does not and will not amount to anything.
I -might go into the imperial conferences that have been held from 1887 to 1932 and show, if I had time, that in all those conferences Canada and the British Empire have stood for certain well-defined and constructive principles. For instance, they opposed the new imperial council formulated and supported by Joseph Chamberlain at one of those conferences-the 1902 meeting. They opposed that and would not accept it, -and rightly so. They also opposed non-negotiation in trade treaties. They wanted to negotiate their own trade treaties, as we do at the present time. That is Liberal policy. They opposed a unitary navy, and our reason for opposing that principle was that we came to the conclusion that by building a Canadian navy we could fight for the empire better than if we backed one empire navy. And that is undeniably the truth. Then we said that without power of negotiation of a trade treaty we would not sign the treaty or accept any responsibility for it, thus showing that we stood for commercial supremecy so far as Canada is concerned, in negotiating treaties with other countries of the world. More than that, we opposed a state church in 1791. The Liberal party opposed an hereditary aristocracy in Canada and drove it out of existence. They opposed irresponsible government by the Family Compact, and also drove that out of existence. We are now going to oppose any economic harnessing of any part of the empire, because if you do that, you will destroy the fiscal

United Kingdom
autonomy of the empire. We are going to drive the government to the country on this question and let the Canadian people judge as to the stand (Liberals have taken in connection with the economic freedom of thi3 dominion.
My time is almost up. I would say that the treaty is discouraging for these reasons: One, it encourages the .principle of a higher protective tariff policy, making reciprocal concessions in the direction of economic nationalism which of course, is the foundation of imperial nationalism, a dangerous ultra-imperial economic narrowness. We oppose that. Two: we oppose the five year term of these treaties because it is vicious, because it limits the negotiable area open to Canada during this period and complicates the process of negotiating new trade treaties with other nations. Three: we oppose the five year term because it is vicious in another direction, nemely, that during this period there is to be no reduction in tariff; the tariff level at its present height is to be maintained-actually increased instead of reduced. Four:	we
oppose the treaty because of its compensatory principle, that is, tariff bonusing of industries that are not efficient, that should not be bonused, and by doing that, destroying trade and adversely affecting the Canadian consumer. Every treaty that Canada enters into should-if based on justice-be followed by an increase in trade and an economic certainty in regard to the future of trade. Viewed in that light, this is a treaty that ought to be repealed because I do not believe it will make any contribution in any of these directions. Five: the high and extensive imperial -preferences render unattainable any move in the direction of freer trade in the future. By nullifying any action in this direction the whole treaty is fraught with danger because it simply stands for higher tariffs and cannot bring about in this nation that economic stability which the present government promised it would secure. Six: it endangers as I have said our constitutional freedom-won after a hundred years of struggle. Seven: it meddles in imperial politics and by such muddling and meddling lays the foundation of the destruction of the empire of our fathers.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that in the critical situation in which Canada finds itself at present, such an important measure as this should have been brought before the House of Commons upon party lines. The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), on October 12, when depositing these four agreements upon the table of the house, used the following words:
These agreements mark the first forward step in a definite scheme of closer empire economic association. They are based upon the principle enunciated by the Conservative party before the last general election, and steadfastly supported by it from that time to the present. They conform to the general plan proposed by this government at the economic conference held at London two years ago, reaffirmed at the opening of the Ottawa conference, and adopted in a very practical way by the agreements which are the outcome of its deliberations.
We are therefore placed in this position: though we admit there are some good features about this treaty-it would be impossible to make a treaty without having some good features in it-it is unfortunate that the defects are more numerous than the good points. It is unfortunate that His Majesty's loyal opposition in this house, representing practically half the population of Canada, should have been debarred from assisting in any way to improve
710	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
our trade relations within the empire. This question has been made a party one. It is said that it conforms to the principles of the Conservative party as enunciated at the Winnipeg convention. The other day listening to a rising young member from Quebec, I was amused to hear him express astonishment that this was being made a party question. He evidently had not read carefully the words of his leader (Mr. Bennett), in which that principle was laid down as a condition that holds today. This merely by way of introduction.
In 1911, some eleven years after I had the honour of being sent here to represent my constituency, the present Prime Minister came into the house as an opponent of reciprocity. Of course he has modified his views somewhat in the case of the St. Lawrence river arrangement, but then he was an out-and-out opponent of all interchange of relations with the United States. I see the hon. member for Argenteuil (Sir George Perley), who sat in the house in those days. He will remember how dangerous it was considered to trade with the United States. At that time I had the honour of presiding over the deliberations in the house when the Hon. Mr. Fielding and the Hon. Mr. Paterson returned from Washington and laid before us the results of their negotiations in the United States capital. For weeks and weeks and even months this question came before us and day after day I put the question to the house, but the Conservative party steadfastly refused to vote on it. They never would consent to divide the house, and finally an appeal was made to the country with the result that we know. But, of course, the whole country did not vote on reciprocity. There were certain provinces which were a unit on reciprocity. In my own province, for example, where the question was not debated at all, the election was won on the question of the navy.
The Prime Minister says that this is the first definite step towards commercial relations with the empire. I shall read his exact words:
These agreements mark the first forward step in a definite scheme of closer empire economic association.
That must have been a slip on the Prime Minister's part because I know he is a well-read man. Besides, in his autobiography it is said that his recreation is reading. He must have read the history of Canada and must know that it was Sir Wilfrid Laurier, who in 1897 made the first definite step towards closer commercial relations with the empire. It was in 1897 that our leader, the then Prime Minister of Canada, Sir Wilfried Laurier, probably the most outstanding figure at the jubilee

after Her Majesty Queen Victoria herself, offered to the British people the first preference that was given by the dominions beyond the seas. I can still remember the complaints from the press gallery and later on on the floor of this house, complaints of all kinds raised by the other side because in giving this preference to England, Canada had received no compensatory advantages. It was forgotten by those who have revived that argument at the present time that at that time the British market was a free market, and so we did not need any preferences; we did not need any tariff reductions, because the whole of our production entered the market of Great Britain on a free entry basis. We therefore did not need and did not want to have any different arrangement than that. Sir Wilfrid Laurier openly declared throughout the country that this was his policy, and the country supported him for many years after that, and to its advantage because the period from 1897 to 1911 was the golden age of Canada in all respects, economically, nationally and socially. Sir Wilfrid Laurier said at the time: We are offering these concessions to Great Britain of our own free will, and we are doing it because it is in the interests of Canada herself; we are asking for nothing in return, but we know that the results will be favourable to Canada. And the results were favourable to Canada. The first preference of 12^ per cent was raised the next year to 25 per cent, and the year following to 33 per cent. Then as if by magic our trade rose by millions and millions, and then by hundreds of millions. The St. Lawrence waterway was converted into one of the finest waterways in the world. Whereas in the olden days a large steamer had to anchor in the lower reaches of the St. Lawrence at sunset, the waterway was developed so that the largest vessels could enter the port of Montreal at midnight as easily as they did under the noonday sun. The whole of Canada was transformed. We passed the autonomy bills notwithstanding the dire opposition of the Conservative party which raised the sectional and religious issues on that great question, but we passed them to the glory of the Liberal party and to the advantage of Canada, and Canada was transformed. In 1911 we went to the country, and on what issue? On the issue of reciprocity. This question of reciprocity is not a new one to those who are familiar with Canadian history. There are now living sons of men who remember that we had reciprocity with the United States which was a mutual advantage to both countries right up to the abrogation of the Elgin treaty in 1866. That treaty

United Kingdom
was probably more advantageous to Canada because it enabled the eastern parts of Canada to obtain their natural market across the line. In those days western Canada did not exist except as part of our geography. It had no representation in this house, nothing beyond the early pioneers, the first settlers, the couriers du bois and the missionaries. But eastern Canada existed, and eastern Canada then was made up of Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island, New Brunswick, Ontario and Quebec. The maritimes, when they were forced into confederation, had then their natural market in the New England states. Boston was then the greatest fish market of the United States, as it is to-day of the .continent of America. When Sir Charles Tupper used to say to the people of the maritime provinces that Halifax would become the new Liverpool of North America he persuaded, nay, almost forced, the people of Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces into confederation. The results of confederation I have no hesitation in saying have not been beneficial to the provinces by the sea. They are losing representation in every parliament of this dominion, and it will be our sad duty again this year to reduce the representation of Nova Scotia, one of the finest provinces in Canada, by two more members. A reduction will also have to be made in the representation of New Brunswick, but Prince Edward Island is saved by that clause which provides that it shall have no fewer representatives in the House of Commons than in the Senate.	.
The breaking of our commercial relations with the United States has been a misfortune to our maritime provinces. In Quebec we have always been favourable to reciprocity and have always advocated it. I remember very well when Mr. W. S. Fielding, probably the most gifted and most talented Finance minister who has ever served Canada, laid his reciprocity proposals on the table of the house. Members flocked around the Speaker's chair. Many Conservative members still living today did not know what to do about it, whether to accept it or not. I remember that Mr. Borden, then the leader of the Conservative party, rose in the house and did not know what stand to take. Why? Because Canada had been advocating reciprocity with the United States for forty years. Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Charles Tupper, Sir Leonard Tilley, and all the stalwarts of the Conservative party had gone year after year on this mission to Washington after the abrogation of the Elgin treaty in 1868 for the purpose of renewing reciprocal relations with the United States. But their efforts were unsuccessful, and then Sir Wilfrid
Laurier came into power, and having secured for Canada the British market, having improved our relations with the empire, having increased the British preference in 1897, 1898 and 1899, in the imperial conference of 1902 he made another proposal, to allow certain goods to be admitted to Canada notwithstanding our tariff at that time. He declared that he was prepared to make modifications in our tariff in favour of the British Empire. Under such circumstances it seems incredible that the Prime Minister should say today:
These agreements mark the first forward step in a definite scheme of closer empire economic association.
He must have entirely forgotten his history. The right hon. gentleman was absent from this house from 1917 to 1925, and when he came back here his views had been somewhat modified by experience, as is the case with all of us. Conditions had changed somewhat. Finally he went to the country as leader of the Conservative party, replacing a very distinguished leader, a very strong man, a man from the west like himself. He went to the country on two questions which could not fail to appeal to a majority of the people. He promised work for the unemployed, and that is the most popular cry on which any man can go to the country at the present time. Witness what is going on now in the United States of America where we are told that fourteen million men are idle as the result of high protection and closed markets. We have got the same thing here. We have raised our tariffs. We did not benefit from the experience of the United States. When the Hawley-Smoot tariff came into effect they received the protests of sixty-seven countries. Notwithstanding that, however, they closed their markets to the world with the result that today there is stagnation of trade. What a spectacle, Mr. Speaker, to find the charitable federation of the city of New York faced with the problem of feeding and clothing a million people. That is the condition of our neighbours. In our own city of Montreal during the summer there were 150,000 unemployed receiving aid from the federal, provincial and municipal governments. How long will this last? Where are we going? Has the world gone mad, and is Canada following in its footsteps?
I see the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), in his seat. I hope before his political career closes he may realize that the policy he is following now is not the one he advocated so strongly, patriotically and successfully on that January day when he had the honour of moving the address in reply which I had the honour
712	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
to second. Today we are the sole survivors of the 250 men who listened to us at that time. The policy of lower tariffs is the policy of the future; the policy of reciprocity is the policy of the future. The League of Nations, which we are sustaining at a cost of from $200,000 to $300,000 per year, and to which we send some of our most distinguished men, has over and over again sounded the warning that high tariffs are practically economic warfare, and that they must be abolished before peaceful conditions may be reestablished in the world. Before any readjustment is brought about the channels to trade must be opened.
We return now to Right Hon. Stanley Baldwin, the man who occupied the most distinguished place at the Imperial economic conference. What did he say? What were his remarks in his opening address? "We have come here to lower tariffs, not to vote to raise them." What I 'most regret in the trade agreement-and I have not time to discuss it at length-is the fact that for five years we are shackled, economically, with Great Britain and the dominions of the empire. We are barred from entering into arrangements with other countries of the world. Let us suppose that Roosevelt wins the election to be held next week in the United States. The Democratic party has always supported lower tariffs and freer international commerce. What would happen if that party asked for a reciprocity arrangement; where would we stand? I shall indicate to the house the difference between the Conservative and the Liberal policies. Today the Conservative party is atempting to tie us down to a five-year agreement.
To indicate what was done at an earlier period in our history, namely in the year 1912, I shall quote from the sessional papers of the parliament of Canada for the first session of the twelfth parliament. At that time a reciprocity arrangement with the United States was under consideration. The following are the words of Mr. W. S. Fielding and Mr. William Paterson addressed to the Secretary of State for the United States:
Nevertheless, it is distinctly understood that we do not attempt to bind for the future the action of the United States congress or the parliament of Canada, but that each of these authorities shall be absolutely free to make any change of tariff policy or of any other matter covered by the present arrangement that may be deemed expedient. We look for the continuance of the arrangement, not because either party is bound to it, but because of our conviction that the more liberal trade policy thus to be established will be viewed by the people of the United States and Canada as one which will strengthen the friendly relations now happily prevailing and promote the commercial interest of both countries.
[Mr. Marcil.l
That was the policy laid down by the Liberal party. They made an agreement with the United States but did not bind that country or Canada for any definite period. The parliament of this country was free to act in the matter, and free to abrogate the treaty if it so desired. If an election were to be held next year or the yeiar after, and after such election the 'Complexion of this house were changed, m what position would we stand? We know the people of Canada are tired of the present regime. Would we be able to negotiate treaties with outside countries? No; the voice of the people would be of no avail; they could ask for a change, but they would not get it. They would find themselves in the same position as hon. members on this side of the house find themselves today. By a ruling of the Speaker the opposition has been prevented from amending the motion before the house; we cannot add a word to it, and we cannot take a word from it. What is the use of all this discussion?

speechtext:
Our
friends opposite try to excuse the government by saying: They had to bargain, they had to make concessions, to get some benefits in return. What are these benefits? I regret to say, notwithstanding the fine picture of it which the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) has given us the other day, that there seems to be none in the agreement that we are now discussing, at least for the farming class which I have the honour to represent in this house.
Mention was made already of this anomaly that whereas the wording of the agreement is very clear and concise as regards manufactured goods, it becomes uncertain and entangled in a lot of conditions and circumlocutions when it deals with farm products. There is nothing but plans and wishes to be carried out in the future, provided that certain things happen. There is nothing done; it is only a project, or if you prefer, a pious wish,
