speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house rose, at six o'clock, I was stating that notwithstanding the rapturous admiration and ecstasies evidenced by our friends opposite for the imperial conference, and such as shown by our friend from Dorchester the other day, the Canadian farmer will remain sceptical. He has the best reasons in the world to be so, for our farming class recall the extraordinary pledges made by the Conservative party at the last election, and which were not carried out. These highly attractive agreements mean nothing to them, and they repose little faith in the realization of these wonderful day dreams which our opponents have in the house.
I fear greatly that this so-called preference granted by the United Kingdom to Canadian products, are delusive and of no benefit to the Canadian farmer, if we consider that Great Britain still maintains an embargo on our potatoes and restrictions on our cattle as our hon. friend from Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) stated a short while ago; if we also consider that the United Kingdom is at present negotiating a treaty with Denmark as regards the exports of bacon and other farming products from the latter country; if we further consider that our lumber is not cut to suit and does not fill the requirements of British importers, according to recent press despatches; and again if we consider that we are thousands of miles from the English market, while the farmers of Ireland, Brittany, Normandy, Belgium, Holland, Denmark, Sweden and Norway, can supply fresh products, as they are only a few hours distant from that market; and lastly if we consider that the depreciation in British currency eliminates the difference in our favour resulting from the preference granted by the trade agreements of the Imperial Economic Conference, at Ottawa.
I am sorry to state that I find nothing in the agreements which might benefit the farmers. On the contrary, I note that owing to these agreements the farmers will pay dearer for their clothes, kitchen utensils, table-service, cutlery, certain building material, paint, glass, pottery, barbed wire, cream and butter separators, carpenter tools, hats, blankets, socks, gloves, leather, chemical fertilizers, farm motors, etc. Why? Because the Ottawa trade agreements served as a pretext to the government so as to raise the tariff on close to 200 classes of manufactured articles which must be purchased by farmers, and because one can rest assured that all tariff increases, on

the whole, mean an increase in the price of such articles. Experience has proved that.
There is one thing which must not be forgotten: The Ottawa trade agreements, even if the wonderful day dreams of our opponents should come true, will not increase trade; they will only divert it. They will not increase it by five cents, they will only result in diverting it into other channels. These agreements will not increase the trade of Canada or the British Empire, but will impede the trade of the Commonwealth with the rest of the world. The situation may be compared to that of a farmer from St. Charles-de-Bellechasse, who grows 100 bushels of potatoes per year and always sells them in St. Gervais, one day he changes his mind and sells them in St. Michel. This would not increase the quantity he had to dispose of, there would be nothing gained by making this change, unless he could obtain a better price for them. I sincerely hope that the farmers may obtain better prices on the British market for their products; however, I have my doubts, because of the reasons just mentioned and the following two: Our farm products, on the British market, will have to compete with the products of the other dominions to which the same preference has been granted; furthermore, I can find nothing in our agreement with the United Kingdom which prevents the latter granting to foreign farm products the same preference as that granted to Canadian products.
I wonder greatly whether before looking for knots in a bulrush and at markets thousands of miles away where our products cannot be shipped without losing their freshness; I wonder, as did the member who has been sitting the longest in the house, the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), whether before concluding an irrevocable and unchangeable agreement for five years, we should not seek to improve our trade relations with our neighbours where our natural market lies. I admit that our neighbours were the first to place obstacles in the reciprocal trade of our products. They will however have a change of government, this is as certain as we will repudiate ours at the next election, and we expect from the next government a broader and more sensible view of the trade relations which should exist between Canada and the United States. The British people seem to have realized this fact. I read in the Droit the other day a statement by Mr. Neville Chamberlain, Chancellor of the Exchequer, of Great Britain, who frankly admitted in the British house recently when discussing the Ottawa agreements:

United Kingdom
Canada had to turn more and more towards the United States and it would have been impossible for her to decline a new offer of reciprocity, which would definitely link her future to that of her great neighbour to the south.
That is why England showed haste to place Canada in the folds and entanglements of the Ottawa trade agreements and made her promise not to disentangle herself for a
period of five years.
It is impossible to find in these agreements the faintest hope for the masses. It is impossible to find anything which might improve the lot of the common people and increase their purchasing power, which after all is the only way to increase our trade. On the contrary, the enforcement of these agreements will mean an increase of restrictions and obstacles to the trade of the products of man's labour. It is nothing less than an unbounded protection in favour of a class of people who were in the habit of making exorbitant profits during the war and now endeavours by cunning intrigues and deceitful legislation to carry on a state of affairs which was abnormal and for the time being.
Hon. gentlemen may make all the agreements they wish; they may increase protection to its very limit; they may increase the tariff until it bursts; they will not succeed in improving the situation as long as they neglect the masses. If the purchasing power of the working and farming classes was increased, if the people had the money to buy, there would be no need to hold conference after conference to activate trade.
To improve the lot of the people and increase their purchasing power, it is necessary to break this concentration of wealth in the hands of a small group and obtain a better distribution of it; we must put an end to the controlling power of money makers over the people and their government itself and not concentrate that power by an exaggerated protection.
As the Holy Father, Pope Pius XI states in his encyclical "Quadragesimo Anno:
In the first place, then, it is patent that in our days not alone is wealth accumulated, but immense power and despotic economic domination is concentrated in the hands of a few and that those few are frequently not the owners, but only the trustees and directors of invested funds, who administer them at their good pleasure.
This power becomes particularly irresistible when exercised by those who, because they hold and control money, are able also to govern credit and determine its allotment, for that reason supplying, so to speak, the life-blood to the entire economic body, and grasping, as 53719-46
it were, in the hands the very soul of production, so that no one dare breathe against their will.

speechtext: It is too bad that statement causes laughter, because it is accurate. Mr. Bruce said: "It will be agreed that tariff arrangements can certainly be destroyed by instability of exchange." The free entry of Canadian products into the British market is useless, at the moment, because Canadian farm products cannot get into that market. They cannot enter the British market because the pound is worth only $3.62. It is useless, and the Canadian farmer knows it. In presenting the agreement the Prime Minister told us that by 1937 we should be able to produce and dispose of 8,500,000 hogs and that by 1942, we should have an export volume of 500,000,000 pounds of bacon and hams. That sounds encouraging on paper but it does not afford much comfort to the hog producer today. He cannot sell bacon and hams in the British market. The other day I had a letter from Peterborough, stating that a certain small abattoir had been trying to put bacon on the British market within the last month and had lost $2 a side or $4 a hog, which is about all the animal is worth at the moment. And in trying to export cattle to the British market now the farmer loses considerably more than $1 per hundredweight. It is all nonsense, and it is an insult to the intelligence of the Canadian people, to bring forward such an arrangement as an encouragement to our farmers. Let me for a moment discuss the Canadian exporter? and I am not speaking now of "peasants" but of honest-to-goodness red-blooded Canadian farmers. When these red-blooded people once come face to face with the type of gentleman who preceded me, the name of whose constituency I do not know, (Mr. LaVergne), I hope, in fact I am sure, they will say to that type of man that parliament would be improved if a "peasant" replaced him.

They want to know how much of these products they wall be able to sell this year, 1932. If the Canadian exporter could send his product to England, even with the pound sterling very low, and buy, in return for his bacon and beef and cheese and wheat, such commodities as woollens and cottons, boots and shoes, cutlery and china, linen and so on, at the same value of the pound sterling as he receives for what he sells, the situation would not be so bad. That would be a fairer arrangement. But the government that has been so very dull on this exchange problem when it applied to exporters of farm products was quick enough on the "uptake" when it affected the Canadian manufacturer. The result is that when we buy woollens and cottons, boots and shoes, and necessities of that kind, in England, we have a fixed valuation of the pound sterling. One certainly gets lost in the maze of fixed valuations, but at any rate the pound for quite a period has been fixed at $4.40. When the duty is charged against the goods, it will be, let us say, 20 per cent against goods valued, not at $4.40 but at the old parity of $4.86f, plus an excise duty of 3 per cent levied on the duty paid value of the goods; and, if the commodity happens to be textiles, there will be an addition in respect of the -weight. In other words, a textile that is heavier and cheaper will pay a higher duty. Furthermore, there will be the new dumping duty. There was an old dumping duty, so that we have now two kinds of duty. I suppose we ought to call them the dumping duties first and second.

CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE MOTION FOR APPROVAL OF TRADE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CANADA AND THE UNITED KINGDOM
speechtext:
Before giving my opinion on the question now before the house, may I say that I have followed with keen interest the discussion on this agreement and the arguments advanced on both sides of the house, and I cannot agree with those who say that this debate should not have taken up as much time as it has. I do not say that the remarks which I shall have the honour to make on behalf of my constituency will advance this debate very far, but it is my duty to express not only the opinion of my constituents but my own opinion as one of the representatives
rMr. Howard.]
of the Canadian people in this house. Although I am ready to agree with the statement made by a great statesman the other day, when he told us that we should not attach too much importance to the letter of the agreement but rather should abide by its spirit, for the sake of this discussion, and in view of the fact that our opponents have gone into the. details of the agreement, I think it is my duty to follow them on their own ground. *
As representing a farming constituency, I had the honour two years ago of a visit on the part of hon. members of this house coming from Ontario. They came as apostles of the policy of protection. They appeared in many counties in the province of Quebec, investigating the agricultural situation in that province. Among them I might mention the horn member for Haldimand, the hon. member for South Hastings and the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe. They came to Laprairie and made an investigation, and, of course; they found that the farmers of my riding, at the price at which they sold their- products, were going to starve. What were the prices of farm products 'at that time? That was during January, 1930. According to Hansard the price of butter in January, 1930, was Z7\, cents, and in April, 1930, 38i. I remember quite well that the hon. member for Haldimand contended in his speech that the herds were decreasing year by year, by reason of butter competition from New Zealand-What do we find after two years of Conservative regime? According to a report dated August, 1932, issued by the Department of Trade and Commerce, dairy herds have decreased by 170,000 head since 1930. The revenue of this industry, which in 1930 was $269,844,000, dropped to $161,243,000, in 1931, a de->
crease of $108,601,000, or forty per cent. This is what has happened during the regime of hon. gentlemen opposite who came into my riding, preaching the doctrine of high protection.
After two years of Conservative administration they come now and ask us to accept this agreement without any discussion. They tell us that as far as the agriculturists are concerned, it will be of great benefit. They claim that they have opened the markets of Great Britain to the farmers of Canada. I should like to deal with that item with which they used to fight us during the last elections *-butter. A preference of fifteen shillings per hundredweight is given by the United Kingdom, which, according to the actual value of the pound sterling, amounts to two cents per pound. In this connection I should like to

United Kingdom
quote the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) as reported at page 647 of Hansard, as follows:
-but the free trade policy of the British government did not give Canadian farmers and manufacturers much chance against foreign competitors located only a few miles from the great markets of London and Liverpool.
The hon. member believes that the protectionist policy of his party is a good one; he believes that this protection of two cents a pound on butter will be beneficial to the farmer. Let us see just where the United Kingdom obtains her butter. I have before me a bulletin dated October 16, 1932, issued by the Department of Agriculture, giving the following information as to 1932 exports to the United Kingdom:
Hundredweight
Denmark	 1,751,108
Australia	 1,149,660
New Zealand	 1,474,265
Canada is not mentioned, so she must come under the heading of "other countries", which exported the small amount of 217,336 hundredweight. The most important country outside of the British Empire exporting butter to the United Kingdom is Denmark, and that country comes within the category mentioned by the hon. member for Dorchester- she is a competitor located only a few miles from the great markets of London and Liverpool. Will we be able to compete with Denmark with a preference of only two cents per pound? How can we compete with New Zealand? According to hon. gentlemen opposite we were unable to compete with that country in 1930 because she was paying a bonus of five cents per pound for each pound of butter exported; how can we then compete with them on the London market?
I am convinced that under these agreements the United Kingdom has obtained more from us than she has given. Hon. friends opposite claim that this agreement is donnant-donnant, or fifty-fifty. In answer to that, I think I need only repeat the story of the butcher who had the reputation of selling the very best grade of sausages. A lady came to him and asked for the recipe and he told her that he made them fifty-fifty with beef and chicken-one bull for one chicken. I ask hon. members opposite: Where is the bull and where is the chicken in the agreement you are asking us to put through this house?
As I said before, to use the language of Lord Reading, the details of these agreements are of no importance whatsoever; it is the principle, the spirit of them which counts in my mind. If this be so, I claim that the principle of these agreements is hidden under the 53719-47
camouflage of tariff policy. What the Prime minister (Mr. Bennett) had in mind is not so much the advantage of trade policy as the advantage of the imperialistic doctrine which is dear to his heart, as dear as it is to the heart of the Right Hon. Neville Chamberlain.
I listened with great interest to the speech delivered the other day by the Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) whom, may I say in passing, I admire very much for his courtesy, for his learning, and for the way in which we are able to approach him. He is a Canadian, and I think in public life there is something dearer to a public man than the party to which he belongs-it is friendship. But I am sure that he will be good enough to allow me to oppose his views so far as political doctrines are concerned. The other day, criticizing the exMinister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) for certain words that he had uttered, the Solicitor General gave a lesson to the ex-Minister of Justice and to my right hon. chieftain (Mr. Mackenzie King). Then he tried to put into the mouth of the late Sir Wilfrid Laurier these words, amongst others:
My dear Ernest, my dear Bill, when you talk about protection and free trade please use the soft pedal and do not make it too thick.
May I say in reply to the Solicitor General that he is making a very big mistake when he contends that the principle underlying these agreements is one of tariff or free trade. What underlies these agreements is the question of imperialism, and this is exactly what we are opposed to. In answer to the Solicitor General, using the same kind of argument as he used and as attributing the words to that distinguished statesman, Sir George Etienne Cartier as the spokesman, I would say to the hon. gentleman: Beware, my young friend, when the jingoes talk tariff and offer you preferences even upon a silver salver; lift up the gift and you will find the serpent of imperialism. You had better apply the four-wheel brakes before it is too late and before the country has gone to perdition.
May I paraphrase the words of the wise in the Trojan war and say to my hon. friend: "Timeo jingoes et dona ferentes," or, in other words: "Beware the jingoes even bringing gifts."
I should like to say a word in reply to what the hon. member for Dorchester said the other day. After quoting Laurier himself, he said that by these agreements:
We have helped the provinces put through their schemes of relief. We have protected the farmers; we have protected the manufacturers; we have protected the consumers, but still the cost of living has been reduced.

738	COMMONS
Imperial Conference-Trade Agreements
Protection! What kind of protection have we had? What kind of protection have our farmers, industrialists and workingmen had? They are starving. They have nothing to live on. They have no money in their pockets. When I heard the hon. member for Dorchester say that his party had given protection to everybody, I was reminded of the fable of Lafontaine about the old man who had a bear for a friend. There was once an old man who, being left alone in the world, was looking for a friend. Walking in the woods one day he met a bear who was in a similar plight. They talked together and the old man treated the bear so well that the latter became his protector. Whatever the old man would do, the bear would follow and watch his master. One very hot summer day the old man was tired, so he lay down under a tree. The bear stood there watching him to see that he was properly protected. It happened that a fly came along and lit on the old man's face, and the bear became mad because he could not with his paw chase away this irritating fly. The bear, becoming madder, took up a stone and, trying to kill the fly while it was on his master's nose, killed his master. That is the kind of protection that our friends the Tories are giving us with these agreements which they are offering to the house. They say protection. Are they giving us protection? The only protection that the jingoes and the Tories have ever given to this country is protection for the rich, the well-to-do, the manufacturers, those who give money to the party to get votes so that after the party is returned to power they may obtain protection.
Hon. gentlemen opposite ask us what is the difference between the Liberal and the Conservative doctrines on imperialism and preferences. To my mind there is a very great difference. I may be wrong; I do not believe that what I am about to say will be swallowed by my opponents as dogma; in fact, I am sure they will not accept it. But I have the right to give my views in answer to their contentions.
In the conference of 1902 the imperialists in the old country had the same intention of inducing the colonies to form a political union, and who was the one who defeated this policy of Chamberlain? It was Sir Wilfrid Laurier. In the Life and Letters of Sir Wilfrid Laurier by 0. D. Skelton, at page 202 I find this:
The conference of 1902 convinced Mr. Chamberlain that the political and the military paths to his goal would give slow progress. He therefore turned to the pathway of trade, along which there had been some greater willingness to walk together. The launching of his imperial preferential trade campaign in 1903

was a direct result of the check in the colonial conference of 1902.	Let Britain adopt a
customs tariff, useful incidentally to protect her own industries and to give bargaining leverage with other powers, and let her grant preferential rates on colonial products in return for concessions on her manufactures, and the British Empire would become self-contained, self-sufficient, bound indissolubly by the ties of common interest.
And here is what is said about Mr. Chamberlain. He said that when the economic union became a fact, "political and military union would follow."
Quoting from page 307 of the same book:
On the tariff question Sir Wilfrid Laurier said little. He agreed in principle vdth Mr. Deakin's eloquent advocacy of imperial preference, but did not wish to interfere in British politics.
There, Mr. Speaker, is the difference between the principles of the Liberal party and the principles of the Conservative party.
The successor of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, with other representatives of this country, went to the conference of 1926, where the same question was again debated. I have before me the report of the Imperial economic committee published by the Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs, in January, 1928. The committee concluded:
That the time is ripe for a national effort to stimulate the consumption of empire produce in the United Kingdom and that this could be effected by the exercise of voluntary preference by the British consumer. The scheme rests on the free will of the individual citizen as consumer.
What do they say about the British consumer?
On the one hand, the purchaser in the old country must be convinced of the desirability of exercising a preference in favour of empire goods, or in other words the housewife must be led to realize that in buying empire produce she is building up employment for her husband and sons. And on the other hand the producer in the empire both in the United Kingdom and overseas must be led to appreciate the fact that he cannot expect the exercise of a preference in his favour if bis goods will not stand competition in regard to price, quality and quantity, or in other words that he has no right to ask the housewife to lay out the family money except to the best advantage of her husband and children.
You find that summed up on the Liberal side in the words of Laurier as imperial solidarity based on local autonomy. Or in the words of our present Liberal chieftain, as expressed by the Imperial economic committee, " the freedom and the liberty of each party to the agreement to handle their own affairs and not to mix up in the other countries' affairs " As is said in the same report:

United Kingdom
Provided that no question which has any reference to another part of the empire may be referred to the committee without the consent of that other part of the empire.
To find out the policy of the Conservative party, shall we go back to the days of Sir John A. Macdonald? No, sir. If we go back to those days we shall find that the opinion of Sir John A. Macdonald was exactly contrary to that of the present Prime Minister. Quoting from page 581 of the Memoirs of Sir John Alexander Macdonald by Sir Joseph Pope, I find that Sir John said:
But, however that might be, I am quite sure that Canada would never consent to be taxed by a central body sitting at London in which she would have practically no voice.
Here is what Sir John A. Macdonald said concerning the tariff policy:
That form of imperial federation is an idle dream. So also in my judgment is the proposal to establish a uniform tariff throughout the empire. No colony would ever surrender its right to control its fiscal policy.
I ask hon. gentlemen opposite what they think of that. Is that in. accordance with the Conservative policy of .today? Sir, the policy of the right hon. Prime Minister and his followers-I say it very seriously if adopted endangers all the principles which we have won since 1837. Among the ninety-two resolutions which were presented to His Majesty in 1837 what do we find? As recorded in Boyd's Life of Sir George Etienne Cartier, page 39:
. . . the imperial parliament, wherein Canada had no representative, had no right to interfere for the renovation of laws which the Canadians considered needful for the maintenance of their rights. At the same time the people's representatives intimated that interference in the local legislation of Canada in any way by British legislatures could only aggravate existing evils.
If these agreements are adopted it means that the British parliament by their representatives are going to dictate to this Canadian parliament how we should increase or decrease tariffs or regulate our fiscal policy.
I said a few moments ago that the only aim of these agreements was a policy of imperialism, and I believe that both Right Hon. Mr. Chamberlain in England and Right Hon. Mr. Bennett in Canada are striving to find out who will win the race in imperialism and imperial matters. During the recent conference they came near to quarrelling because each one wanted to be the first to have these policies adopted. In the Montreal Standard of Saturday last we find this statement:
It is becoming clearer every day that the real strong man in the government is Right Hon. Neville Chamberlain. The gap between his 53719-17^
opinions and those of Mr. Baldwin is becoming more and more evident as the present session of parliament proceeds. . . .
Chamberlain has the advantage of knowing precisely what he wants, and he is equally determined to get it. He is as ardent a protectionist and imperialist as Mr. Amery. He feels it his duty to carry out the mission of his famous, father. He is also a stern economist.
And further the article proceeds:
Mr. Baldwin is a link between Mr. MacDonald and Mr. Chamberlain, and, with characteristic sincerity and honesty, he is trying to preserve the national character of the government and not let it become an administration dominated by Chamberlain and his Tory supporters.

Mr. C. DUMAINE (Bagot) (Translation) r Mr. Speaker, may I, first, sincerely congratulate the hon. member for Laprairie Napierville (Mr. Dupuis), who has made such a splendid speech and who so forcibly expressed his opposition to the resolution under consideration. May I also extend the same congratulations to the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Howard), to the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Boulanger) and to the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil), all of whom delivered such splendid speeches, this day. I feel rather shy in rising, after such distinguished speakers, to express my views as regards this resolution which is being discussed in the house.
I must admit there is not much to be added to this debate, because many members have threshed out this question. It has been studied from all angles and truly, if the members opposite had not endeavoured to prove to the house, the ratepayers and the people the benefits to be derived from the agreements entered into at the Imperial Economic Conference of 1932, it would be unnecessary to add anything further as regards these agreements with the United Kingdom and the Dominions. I shall be brief, because I have little faith in these agreements and, in my opinion, they are not even worth criticizing. However, this pact brings up an important question, namely that of imperialism, and if I raise my voice this evening it is to uphold the rights of Canadian farmers of my county and express, personally, my views.
May I first point out, sir, that many items under the trade agreements entered into with the United Kingdom comprise no changes and are therefore the same as they were previous to the Imperial Conference of 1932. There are, however, a number of items that indicate a decrease in duties. I shall quote items 146, 147, 152, 156 and 164 in connection with wine,

beers, porters and alcohol to which British preference extends and on which prices will be lowered. Was preference granted on these articles as somewhat of a consolation to the people of this country?

I trust not because our people have no need of this beverage to drown their sorrow. On a number of items which are indispensible to the farming class, such as separators and barbed wire the tariff was increased by 25 per cent. It was thought proper, in these trade agreements, not to lower, but rather increase the tariff on articles principally purchased by the poor classes-I can state that the latter include the farming and working classes. A decrease of duty is mentioned on cotton. The duties are lowered on the better quality of cottons: those that we, the poor, cannot afford to purchase; the duties were also lowered on fine linen goods, first quality, which are bought by wealthy people, and which the poor cannot afford.
In these trade agreements, the poor consumer is ignored, and the interests of the industrialist, capitalist and stock-holders whose life is one of pleasure, are looked after. That is as regards industry, trade and finance, as a whole, the tariff was fixed at so much per cent on each item. But, what was done for the agricultural class? Our hon. friends opposite state: the Imperial conference affords all the guarantees possible for the sale of farm products, and the farmers of this country Will greatly benefit in this respect. Yet, there is not a farm product on which a tariff duty was fixed and for which a market is guaranteed or a reasonable price equal to that of production, is assured.
The London market was thrown open for our butter. I have very little faith in the London market, because we shall have to compete with New Zealand and Australia which can produce butter and export it to the English market on better terms and at a lower price than we can. Do you recall, Sir, when the election of 1930 took place, Canada levied a duty of 1 cent per pound and our opponents contended that we could not compete with New Zealand and that Australia and the former country were stealing pur markets away from us. In my opinion this agreement is certainly not advantageous for the farming class of Quebec or the other provinces.
May I ask the hon. gentlemen opposite whether they have found a market for our hay. There is a large quantity of good hay

grown in my county. We cannot find a market. Our farmers would greatly benefit had they a market for this hay. A number of farmers in my constituency have at present, two or three hundred tons of hay in their barns and are unable to find any outlet for it. Do the new agreements of the Imperial conference give us a market for our hay? There is nothing in them which will be in any way advantageous to us. Have they found a market for our potatoes? Nothing in those agreements give us any hope of disposing of our potato crop. The same may be said for all our farm products. For instance, with reference to bacon, we are told: We open the great London markets to you. This market may, perhaps, be opened to us, but we are not told what price will be offered for our bacon. In my opinion, the farming class was ignored at the Imperial economic conference. A few days previous to the conference, the Prime Minister refused to meet the farmers of this country and to even grant them five minutes of his time. I think that he is still following the same tactics and policy.
I find no advantages in the resolutions under consideration and as the representative of a beautiful farming county I shall register my vote against these agreements, because I love my country and wish to carry out my pledges, as a member, to the very end.
